lesson.title: A Faster Road to the Same Destination: Catalysts and Equilibrium
lesson.summary: Because a catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions by exactly the same factor, it helps a reversible reaction reach equilibrium faster without shifting the equilibrium position or changing the value of the equilibrium constant, K.
lesson.body:
At equilibrium, the forward rate and the reverse rate are equal. A catalyst lowers Ea for the forward reaction and Ea for the reverse reaction by the identical amount, since both are measured relative to the same transition state peak on the energy diagram, and lowering that one peak affects both directions equally. Because the forward and reverse rate constants both increase by the same multiplicative factor, their ratio, which is exactly the equilibrium constant K, stays completely unchanged. The practical consequence is precise and testable: a catalyst gets a reversible reaction to equilibrium faster, but it has no effect whatsoever on where that equilibrium sits, meaning the equilibrium concentrations and the value of K are exactly the same with or without the catalyst present.

This is worth contrasting directly with the factors covered under chemical equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle. Changing concentration, changing pressure or volume, or changing temperature can all genuinely shift where an equilibrium lies, and changing temperature actually changes the value of K itself, since those are real thermodynamic effects. A catalyst does none of this. It does not appear anywhere in the equilibrium expression, and it does not change delta G, delta H, or K. Its effect is purely kinetic, about the path and the speed of getting to equilibrium, never about where equilibrium ends up.

The Haber process, N2 gas plus 3H2 gas in equilibrium with 2NH3 gas, illustrates why this distinction matters in the real world. At a given temperature, the equilibrium constant K and the resulting equilibrium yield of ammonia are fixed by thermodynamics alone, completely independent of whether the iron catalyst used industrially is present. Without any catalyst, this reaction is so slow at the moderate temperatures where the equilibrium yield is favorable that reaching equilibrium would take an impractically long time, essentially useless for a chemical plant that needs to produce ammonia continuously. Adding the iron catalyst does not improve the equilibrium yield at all, but it allows the system to actually reach that same fixed equilibrium composition within the residence time of a real industrial reactor. This is exactly why industrial chemists still care intensely about finding good catalysts even knowing a catalyst can never push the equilibrium yield higher: without one, a thermodynamically favorable process can be commercially worthless simply because it is too slow, and the catalyst is what makes the process viable at all, while the actual product yield ceiling remains set by temperature and pressure, the genuine equilibrium controlling factors, not by the catalyst.

Given how often this is tested and misunderstood, it is worth stating plainly one more time: a catalyst does not increase the amount of product present at equilibrium, and it does not change K. It changes only how quickly the system arrives at the same equilibrium it would have reached anyway, given enough time.
